question: Santa Claus is based on a real bishop called Nicholas, who lived about 1,700 years ago in a warm town by the Mediterranean Sea. In which modern country is that town?
source_excerpt: Bishop of Myra, a city in Lycia in the Roman Empire. Today that region is in Turkey, Antalya Province.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Santa as northern: Lapland, the North Pole, maybe the Netherlands. The man who inspired him lived on a sunny Mediterranean coast in what is now Turkey.
extra.verification_notes: Nicholas was Bishop of Myra in Lycia, now Demre in Antalya Province, Turkey (c. 270–343 AD); no conflicting sources found.

explanation: Nicholas was bishop of Myra, now the town of Demre on Turkey's southern coast. The original Santa lived among olive trees, not snowdrifts.

question: In the Netherlands, Santa's Dutch cousin Sinterklaas doesn't come from the North Pole. He arrives every November by steamboat. From which country does he sail?
source_excerpt: the festivities begin in mid-November, when Sinterklaas "arrives" by a steamboat at a designated seaside town, supposedly from Spain.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a Christmas gift-bringer comes from somewhere cold and northern. The Dutch Sinterklaas sails up from sunny Spain.
extra.verification_notes: Sinterklaas traditionally arrives by steamboat from Spain each November, per the St. Nicholas Center; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Dutch tradition says Sinterklaas spends the year in Spain and arrives by steamboat in mid-November. His arrival is broadcast live on national TV.

question: The famous poem 'Twas the Night Before Christmas names eight of Santa's reindeer. Which reindeer, now the most famous of all, is not in it?
source_excerpt: Santa's sleigh is pulled by eight reindeer

extra.why_interesting: Rudolph feels like the most essential reindeer of all, so players assume he was always there. He is missing from the poem that named Santa's team, and he started out as a department-store promotion.
extra.verification_notes: The poem names eight reindeer (Dasher, Dancer, Prancer, Vixen, Comet, Cupid, Donder, Blitzen) and Rudolph, created in 1939, is not among them; nothing newer changes this.

explanation: Rudolph was invented more than a century later, in 1939, for a free booklet handed out by an American department store.

question: Legend says the real St Nicholas secretly tossed bags of gold through a poor family's window at night, and the gold landed in something left drying by the fire. What was it? Children still hang them up at Christmas.
topic: St Nicholas and how he became Santa Claus
source_excerpt: the gold landed in the stockings, which were hanging by the fireplace to dry

extra.why_interesting: Players hang Christmas stockings every year without wondering why. It turns out the custom goes back to a 4th-century bishop's secret gift, so a familiar household ritual becomes a 1,700-year-old story.
extra.verification_notes: The legend's gold landing in stockings drying by the fire is the standard origin of the Christmas stocking; some versions say shoes, but the 'hang them up' clue fits stockings (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_stocking).

explanation: The gold was dowry money for the man's three daughters, and that is why Christmas stockings get hung up by the fireplace. The same three bags of gold are behind the three golden balls on a pawnbroker's sign, since Nicholas is also their patron saint.

question: Today a British mince pie is a sweet pastry full of raisins and spice. But centuries ago, what was actually minced to go inside it?
source_excerpt: Meat was gradually dropped over the nineteenth century, so modern mincemeat contains dried fruit, nuts, apples, spices, and brandy or vinegar, but no meat.

extra.why_interesting: Players treat a mince pie as a sweet fruit pastry and never question the name; realising 'mince' literally meant chopped meat is a satisfying 'of course' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Mince pies historically contained minced meat (beef, mutton, tongue, pork) plus suet, dropped gradually in the 19th century, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mince_pie

explanation: Early mince pies held chopped mutton or beef cooked with fruit and spices. The meat slowly vanished, but the beef fat called suet still turns up in many mincemeat recipes.

question: In Britain, families mix their Christmas pudding on 'Stir-up Sunday'. But the name doesn't come from the pudding. It comes from the first words of what?
source_excerpt: Stir up, we beseech thee, O Lord, the wills of thy faithful people...

extra.why_interesting: Everyone assumes the name describes stirring the pudding batter; in fact the pudding custom borrowed its name from the opening words of a church prayer.
extra.verification_notes: Stir-up Sunday is named for the opening words of the collect ('Stir up, we beseech thee, O Lord...') in the Book of Common Prayer, which is a church prayer.

explanation: The prayer read in Anglican churches that Sunday begins 'Stir up, we beseech thee, O Lord'. It fell on just the right weekend to give the puddings a few weeks to mature, so the name stuck to the kitchen.

question: Eggnog once caused a real riot. Cadets at America's most famous army academy smuggled in whiskey for their Christmas eggnog, and the party went badly wrong. Which academy?
source_excerpt: A drunken Christmas eggnog party in the North Barracks grew into a riot that lasted until Christmas morning and involved more than a third of the cadets.

extra.why_interesting: Eggnog is the cosy, harmless Christmas drink, and military academies stand for discipline. The clash is funny, and 'America's most famous army school' gives a reachable path to the name.
extra.verification_notes: The Eggnog Riot of 24–25 December 1826 occurred at the US Military Academy at West Point after cadets smuggled in whiskey for their Christmas eggnog.

explanation: Alcohol was banned, so cadets sneaked in several gallons of whiskey. By Christmas morning they were smashing windows, and around twenty cadets were court-martialled.

question: Christmas crackers were invented in Victorian London. Before the bang, the paper hats and the jokes were added, the idea began as a twist of paper wrapped around what?
alternative_answers: a sweet with a love message
source_excerpt: he came across the French 'bonbon', a sugared almond wrapped in a twist of tissue paper.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a cracker as a paper tube holding a hat, a bad joke and a plastic toy, and assume that was always it. In fact the whole thing started as fancy sweet wrapping, and the bang, hat and toy were added later. The twisted-end shape is a clue a player can reason from, because it looks like a wrapped sweet.
extra.verification_notes: Tom Smith's original product was a French-style bonbon (sugared almond/sweet) in a twist of tissue paper, later adapted into the cracker, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Smith_(confectioner).

explanation: London confectioner Tom Smith copied the French bonbon, a sugared almond in twisted paper. He later added a love note and then the bang, reportedly inspired by the crackle of a log fire.

question: In 1965, two astronauts told Mission Control they'd spotted something like Santa in orbit. Then they pulled out a smuggled harmonica and bells and played the first song ever played on instruments in space. Which song?
source_excerpt: Sixty years ago, when instruments were played in space for the first time, it was Jingle Bells all the way

extra.why_interesting: Players think of space music as something grand or scientific. The first live performance up there was a cheeky sleigh-ride tune on a pocket harmonica, after a fake 'UFO sighting' prank on Mission Control.
extra.verification_notes: Gemini 6A's Schirra and Stafford played Jingle Bells on harmonica and bells on Dec 16, 1965, after the Santa 'UFO' report; Smithsonian and Guinness agree.

explanation: The Gemini 6 crew snuck the harmonica and bells aboard, and both instruments are now kept at the Smithsonian.

question: When Silent Night was first sung in a village church in Austria, the organ wasn't used. Instead, the young priest who wrote the words accompanied the singers himself. What instrument did he play?
source_excerpt: Joseph Mohr took the tenor part and played guitar, while Franz Xaver Gruber sang bass.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone pictures the most solemn church carol sung with a grand organ. It actually debuted with a humble folk instrument played by the priest himself.
extra.verification_notes: Mohr sang tenor and played guitar at the 1818 premiere per stillenacht.at; the organ-damage reason is disputed but the question doesn't depend on it.

explanation: Franz Gruber set Joseph Mohr's poem for two voices and guitar, an instrument many people at the time thought belonged in taverns rather than churches.

question: Forget Elvis, the Beatles and Elton John. According to Guinness World Records, the best-selling single of all time is a Christmas song sung by Bing Crosby. Which one?
alternative_answers: I'm Dreaming of a White Christmas
source_excerpt: is considered to be the best-selling physical single of all time with an estimated 50 million copies sold.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the all-time single sales record belongs to a pop or rock megahit like Elvis, the Beatles or Elton John. It actually belongs to a gentle 1940s crooner's Christmas ballad.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness World Records lists Bing Crosby's 'White Christmas' as the best-selling physical single of all time (~50 million), and no newer record has displaced it.

explanation: Crosby's recording has sold an estimated 50 million copies. It was written by Irving Berlin, a Jewish immigrant who grew up without celebrating Christmas.

question: Old Hollywood snow was often made from cornflakes, but they crunched too loudly for the actors' lines. For It's a Wonderful Life, the crew mixed a quiet snow from a foam chemical instead. Which safety device normally sprays that foam?
source_excerpt: The mixture used foamite from fire extinguishers with sugar and water, distributed by a wind machine

extra.why_interesting: Nobody thinks about what fake movie snow is made of; the crunchy-cornflakes problem is a delightful setup, and the answer can be reasoned out because foam is the obvious quiet, white material.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources confirm RKO's It's a Wonderful Life snow used Foamite, the fire-extinguisher foam, replacing noisy painted cornflakes (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/crazy-tricks-early-filmmakers-used-fake-snow-180961522/).

explanation: The crew mixed fire-extinguisher foam with soap, sugar and water, which gave silent snow that could be sprayed by the ton, and the trick won a technical award.

question: True or false: the black-and-white gangster movie Kevin plays in Home Alone, the one with the line 'Keep the change, ya filthy animal', is a real film from Hollywood's golden age.
source_excerpt: For the film within a film, Angels with Filthy Souls (the title of which parodies the 1938 crime film Angels with Dirty Faces), shooting took one day... To create the illusion that the film was an authentic 1940s gangster film, the scene was filmed on black-and-white negative film

extra.why_interesting: Many viewers assume it is a real 1930s or 1940s classic because it looks so authentic. Learning it was made for the film overturns years of rewatching.
extra.verification_notes: Angels with Filthy Souls is a fictional film-within-a-film created for Home Alone, parodying the real 1938 film Angels with Dirty Faces, so 'False' is correct.

explanation: False. 'Angels with Filthy Souls' was shot just for Home Alone as a spoof of the 1938 classic 'Angels with Dirty Faces'.

question: In The Muppet Christmas Carol, Michael Caine plays Scrooge and Kermit plays Bob Cratchit. Which Muppet plays the story's author, Charles Dickens, as narrator?
source_excerpt: Dave Goelz performs Gonzo, who plays Charles Dickens and serves as narrator.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect Kermit to have the big role. The fact that the author himself is played by Gonzo, a strange blue creature, is a funny twist that fans can recall and others can reach by eliminating the main Muppets.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's cast list gives Gonzo as Charles Dickens (Narrator) in The Muppet Christmas Carol, and I found no newer development that changes this.

explanation: Gonzo the Great narrates as Dickens, with Rizzo the Rat at his side questioning whether a blue weirdo could really be the famous author.

question: In Catalonia, children feed a smiling wooden log for weeks and tuck it under a blanket. On Christmas they hit it with sticks until it delivers sweets. How does the log deliver them?
source_excerpt: children feed and keep the log warm so that it will defecate presents on Christmas

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a gentle Yule log tradition; the reveal that the log delivers presents by pooping them out is pure delighted disbelief. The stem gives footholds (feeding, blanket, hitting it), so a sharp player can reason to it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Tió de Nadal article confirms the log is fed, covered with a blanket, beaten with sticks, and then 'defecates' the gifts.

explanation: The log is called Caga Tió, roughly 'pooping log', and the song the children sing while beating it orders it to poop out treats.

question: Icelandic children put a shoe on the windowsill before Christmas so the Yule Lads can leave sweets in it. Naughty children don't get coal. What do they find instead?
source_excerpt: disobedient children will instead find a rotten potato in their shoes.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect coal, the familiar punishment from other traditions; Iceland's version is a rotten potato, which is a satisfying near-miss for anyone who guesses coal.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms disobedient children find a rotten potato in their shoes instead of a gift; no newer developments found.

explanation: There are 13 mischievous Yule Lads, arriving one per night, and a rotten potato in the shoe is their verdict on bad behaviour.

question: In Japan, where few people are Christian, a 1970s advertising campaign made Christmas dinner from one American fast-food chain a national custom. Families book their meals well in advance. Which chain?
source_excerpt: A successful advertising campaign in the 1970s made eating at KFC around Christmas a national custom. Its chicken meals are so popular during the season that stores take reservations months in advance.

extra.why_interesting: A fast-food chain as the centrepiece of a national Christmas dinner sounds absurd; many players will have heard of it and enjoy the instant recognition, while the advert origin is the payoff.
extra.verification_notes: KFC's Christmas Party Barrel pre-order tradition in Japan continues in 2026, with reservations opened Nov 11 and pickup Dec 19-25; see https://www.arabnews.com/node/2624851/offbeat

explanation: It all started with a 1970s advertising slogan, 'Kentucky for Christmas!', and fried chicken has been Japan's festive meal ever since.

question: Today tinsel is cheap and shiny plastic. But when it was first made in Germany about four hundred years ago, it was cut from thin strips of which precious metal?
source_excerpt: originally made from extruded strands of silver

extra.why_interesting: Players picture tinsel as cheap plastic fluff, so learning it started as a luxury of real precious metal is a nice twist. The colour and sparkle give a fair path to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms tinsel was originally made from silver, first produced in Nuremberg, Germany around 1610.

explanation: Real silver tarnished black in candlelight, which is one reason cheaper metals and eventually plastic took over.

question: Every Christmas, the giant tree in London's Trafalgar Square arrives as a thank-you gift from Norway. Which Norwegian city sends it?
source_excerpt: Since 1947, Oslo has gifted a Christmas tree to London as a symbolic thank-you for the support Britain gave Norway during World War II.

extra.why_interesting: Many people know the tree comes from Norway, but fewer know that one specific city gives it. The capital is a reachable guess, so the question rewards a confident hunch.
extra.verification_notes: Oslo has gifted the Trafalgar Square tree annually since 1947, and the 2025 and 2026 trees also come from Oslo (https://www.oslo.kommune.no/english/politics/the-city-council/the-mayor/the-trafalgar-square-christmas-tree/).

explanation: Oslo has sent a spruce every year since 1947, chosen from the forests around the city and decorated in simple Norwegian style with vertical strings of white lights.

question: Prince Albert gets the credit for making the Christmas tree fashionable in Britain. But decades earlier, another royal had already decorated one at Windsor. Who was it?
topic: Prince Albert and the royal Christmas tree
source_excerpt: Queen Charlotte set up the first known English tree at Queen's Lodge, Windsor, in December, 1800.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone credits Prince Albert with the British Christmas tree, so a royal tree at Windsor decades earlier overturns that belief. The multiple-choice format makes it winnable: a player who knows that Charlotte was German can reason their way to her.
extra.verification_notes: Queen Charlotte is widely credited with the first known royal Christmas tree in England at Queen's Lodge, Windsor, in December 1800, and the other options do not fit.

explanation: Queen Charlotte grew up in Germany and brought the custom with her. Albert's tree became famous later because a magazine printed a picture of the royal family gathered around it.

question: The very first Advent wreath was made by a Hamburg pastor for children who kept asking how long it was until Christmas. He built it from an old piece of farm equipment. Which one?
source_excerpt: children at the mission school Rauhes Haus, founded by Wichern in Hamburg, would ask daily if Christmas had arrived... he took a large wooden ring from an old cartwheel

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the wreath as always having been a small evergreen ring with four candles on a table. Its first version was a huge recycled farm wheel holding a candle for every day, built to answer impatient children.
extra.verification_notes: Wichern's 1839 Rauhes Haus Advent wheel is widely documented as made from an old cartwheel (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advent_wreath); the candle-count variations don't affect the answer.

explanation: It held a candle for every day of Advent, small ones for weekdays and big ones for Sundays. Later the wreath was shrunk to just the four Sunday candles we know today.

question: Nuremberg's famous Christmas market is opened by a figure called the 'Christ Child'. It isn't a baby and it isn't a boy. Who plays the role?
source_excerpt: The Christkind must be 16 to 19 years old, at least 1.60 meters tall and not afraid of heights.

extra.why_interesting: 'Christ Child' makes players think of a baby or a little boy. The real answer is a teenage girl with golden curls and a crown, which overturns the image.
extra.verification_notes: Nuremberg's Christkind is a young woman aged 16-19 per the official tourism site; no newer development contradicts 'a teenage girl'.

explanation: Every two years Nuremberg chooses a young woman, usually 16 to 19, to wear the golden wig and crown. She opens the market with a poem from a church balcony.

question: Nuremberg's Christmas market sells little people made of dried fruit, with a walnut for a head. Their arms and legs are made from which fruit?
source_excerpt: prunes serve as limbs, figs make up the body, and walnuts, the smoother the better, form the head

extra.why_interesting: The stem tells players the figures are made of dried fruit, so they can reason through the usual dried fruits and work out which is small and oval enough for limbs. The image of edible little people made of prunes is the delight.
extra.verification_notes: Official Christkindlesmarkt site confirms prune men have prunes as limbs, figs as body, and a walnut head; no newer developments contradict this.

explanation: They are called 'prune men' in the local dialect, and figs usually make the body. Buying one is said to bring good luck and money for the year ahead.

question: Mistletoe is famous for Christmas kisses, but in the wild you'll never see it growing out of the ground. So where does it grow?
source_excerpt: Mistletoes are obligate hemiparasitic plants that attach to a host tree or shrub by a haustorium, from which they draw water and nutrients.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has seen mistletoe hung over a doorway but few think about where it actually grows. Most picture a shrub on the ground, but it lives high in the branches of other trees and feeds off them.
extra.verification_notes: Christmas mistletoe (Viscum album/Phoradendron) is a hemiparasite growing on host tree branches; terrestrial exceptions like Nuytsia are not the Christmas mistletoe, so the pair stands.

explanation: Mistletoe is a parasite that taps into a host tree's branches for water and nutrients. Birds spread it by eating the sticky berries and leaving the seeds on the next branch.

question: Some people think 'Xmas' is a lazy modern shortcut. In fact the X is a letter from another alphabet. Which one?
source_excerpt: The 'X' comes from the Greek letter Chi, which is the first letter of the Greek word Christós.

extra.why_interesting: Many people think 'Xmas' is a lazy modern shortcut, or even a deliberate removal of Christ from Christmas. In fact the X is a Greek letter standing for Christ, so the abbreviation is ancient and religious in origin.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the X in Xmas is the Greek letter chi, the first letter of Christos.

explanation: The X is the Greek letter chi, the first letter of 'Christos', meaning Christ. Scribes were using the X shorthand for Christ more than a thousand years ago.

question: In 'The Twelve Days of Christmas', the true love repeats every earlier gift on each new day. Count everything delivered over all twelve days. How many gifts is that?
source_excerpt: persona's true love sends them a total of 364 items by the twelfth day

extra.why_interesting: Players know the song but rarely add it up. Most anchor on the 78 gifts listed in the final verse, but because the gifts repeat each verse, the true total is 364, one for almost every day of the year.
extra.verification_notes: Sum of triangular numbers for days 1–12 is 364, matching Wikipedia's stated total.

explanation: It comes to 364, one present for nearly every day of the year. The 78 is the trap, because that is only what's listed in the final verse.

question: The first Christmas card sold in shops, in London in 1843, showed a family at a festive table, and it is said to have shocked some people. What was the little girl in the picture doing?
source_excerpt: allegedly the image of the family drinking wine together proved controversial

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the very first Christmas card to be pious or cosy. In fact it caused a small scandal because it showed a little girl sipping wine with the grown-ups.
extra.verification_notes: The 1843 Cole/Horsley card showed a family, including a child, drinking wine, which upset temperance campaigners; the sources are not precise about the little girl herself, and Wikipedia only says the family drinking wine was controversial (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_card).

explanation: The card showed the whole family raising glasses, and a small child was having a sip of wine too. Temperance campaigners were not amused.
